rated_messages.input_message: What can you do right now to break the automatic habit of smoking to help you feel better? Pause. Close your eyes. And take 10 slow breaths.

When smoking, it can feel like your hands are for holding a cigarette, your mouth is for smoking the cigarette, and your chest and lungs need to breathe in the smoke. Spend 3 minutes noticing how your hands feel, how your mouth feels, and how your chest feels. The more you practice noticing these things without smoking, the sooner your body will stop being a trigger for you.
Life can get you really stressed out, but turning to cigs isn't the answer. Call or text family and friends instead. Ask them to help you stay on track.
You spent a long time training your brain to want a cig. Now you're retraining your brain, and it's natural that this might take time.

Think of urges as loud construction noises. Sometimes there's nothing you can do except agree that it's annoying. If you fight it, you feel more irritated, right? Let your urge be there until it passes on its own.
Take a slow, deep breath in. And let it out. Now, ask yourself, "Am I willing to go one minute without smoking?" When that minute is over, ask yourself this question again.
Ask yourself, "What do I need right now? Is it really a smoke, or is there something else I need? How can I best take care of myself right now?"

It's quite common for people to try and give themselves reasons for having 'just one' when they start working on quitting smoking. If you have these thoughts, let them happen, then picture yourself putting them into a hot-air balloon and watch them float away.

Some people find it helpful to give a name to their urge. If you're experiencing regular urges, give that feeling a name ('Olga the urge'?), and tell it that you won't give in to it. It may make it easier to live with (e.g. "ok Olga, I need to be by myself now...").
